quests.scene: At a job interview, the interviewer greets you: 'Good morning, I'm Ms. Okafor. Thanks for coming in.'
options: Good morning, Ms. Okafor. Thank you for having me.
Hey, nice to meet you! Cool office.
Morning! Just call me Sam, there's really no need to be so formal with each other.
Hi. So, what do I need to do first?
quests.hint: Match her level of formality; she hasn't invited first names.
quests.explanation: Using her title and thanking her mirrors her tone and shows respect. Overly casual replies or presuming first names can weaken a first impression before the interview starts.
quests.culturalNote: In many English-speaking workplaces, waiting for someone to offer their first name is safer in formal first meetings.

quests.scene: At a work event, your manager Ms. Reyes joins you and your friend Jo, who has never met her. You need to introduce them.
options: Jo, meet my boss.
This is Jo. She's just a friend, don't mind her.
Ms. Reyes, this is my friend Jo. Jo, Ms. Reyes is my manager.
Ms. Reyes, meet Jo. She's here with me.
quests.hint: In introductions, give each person a name and a link to you.
quests.explanation: Naming both people and explaining how each connects to you lets them start talking. Vague or dismissive introductions leave one person unsure what to say.
quests.culturalNote: Traditionally the more senior person's name is said first; the key is that both names and roles are clear.

quests.scene: You're emailing a professor you've never met to ask about joining her lab. Her name is Dr. Malik.
options: Hi Malik, wanted to pick your brain about your lab.
To whom it may concern, I have a question about your lab and whether I could visit sometime soon.
Hey! Can you tell me about your lab?
Dear Dr. Malik, I'm a second-year student at Kent, writing to ask about your lab.
quests.hint: A first email needs the right title and a reason for writing.
quests.explanation: Using her title and stating who you are and why you're writing gets her attention politely. Casual or impersonal openers can seem careless.
quests.culturalNote: Academic emails typically use titles until invited otherwise, and state the purpose in the first line.

quests.scene: You've chatted with a man at your gym twice, but his name has slipped your mind. He waves and approaches.
options: Nice to see you again, buddy.
Have we met before?
You look really familiar. Did we meet at some point, maybe at the pool or something?
I'm sorry, your name has slipped my mind — could you remind me?
quests.hint: Honesty about forgetting works better than pretending.
quests.explanation: Admitting it briefly and asking is respectful and quickly resolves the issue. Pretending or acting like you've never met can offend when you've actually talked.
quests.culturalNote: Most people are sympathetic about forgetting names; a quick admission is usually forgiven.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: In a meeting, a colleague mispronounces your name, Shanni, as 'Shan-eye.'
options: That's not my name.
Just call me Sam, everyone does — it's simpler for everybody, and I don't mind at all.
It's actually 'Shah-NEE' — no worries, it's easy to mix up.
Don't worry, it's not important.
quests.hint: Correct it kindly so it doesn't happen again.
quests.explanation: A friendly correction avoids embarrassment and helps them get it right later. Ignoring it or offering a nickname means it will likely keep happening.
quests.culturalNote: Correcting pronunciation early is normal and usually appreciated.

quests.scene: A colleague named Anjali corrects you after you pronounced her name wrong at a team lunch.
options: Whatever, close enough.
Oh, I've heard it said both ways.
Sorry, your name is really hard to say.
Sorry — Anjali, got it. Thanks for telling me.
quests.hint: Thank her for the correction, don't defend the mistake.
quests.explanation: A brief apology and thanks acknowledge the error and show you'll try again. Excuses or blaming the name make her feel it was her fault.
quests.culturalNote: Names carry personal significance; getting them right is a basic courtesy.

quests.scene: You've just moved into an apartment building and want to introduce yourself to the neighbor across the hall.
options: Hello. Do you mind keeping the noise down?
I'm the new tenant. Which bins do we use?
Hi, I'm Lena from number 6 — just moved in. I brought some cookies to say hello.
Hi neighbour, I'm having a party next weekend, hope that's okay.
quests.hint: A first meeting is about connection, not requests or warnings.
quests.explanation: Introducing yourself with a small gesture builds goodwill. Opening with a complaint, chore, or warning makes the first impression transactional or negative.
quests.culturalNote: Bringing a small gift when meeting neighbors is common in some places but not necessary everywhere.

quests.scene: You've just been added to a cycling club group chat with forty strangers. You want to say something first.
options: Why was I added to this?
Hi.
Hi all, I'm Ben — thanks for adding me. Looking forward to the next ride.
So when is the next ride, where do we meet, and who is bringing the snacks and spare tubes?
quests.hint: Say hello and who you are before asking anything.
quests.explanation: Introducing yourself and showing enthusiasm makes you approachable. Jumping into logistics or questioning the invitation feels off.
quests.culturalNote: Group chats usually welcome short self-introductions; lurking silently can feel odd to others.

quests.scene: You join a video call and the host says, 'Welcome — have we met?' You started on Monday.
options: We haven't yet — I'm Tara, I joined the finance team on Monday.
I'm Tara.
Not really, I only joined to listen in today, so please don't worry about introducing me to anyone.
Yes, obviously, I sit two desks from you.
quests.hint: Answer the question, then give useful context about yourself.
quests.explanation: Giving your name and role helps the host and others place you. A bare name or sarcasm doesn't help, and claiming to be silent wastes the introduction.
quests.culturalNote: New joiners often introduce themselves with a role; it saves colleagues asking later.

quests.scene: At a wedding, the stranger sitting next to you asks, 'How do you know the bride?' You studied with her.
options: Why do you ask?
Through friends.
That's a personal question.
We studied together years ago. How about you?
quests.hint: Answer honestly and give the conversation somewhere to go.
quests.explanation: A direct answer plus a return question keeps small talk alive. Suspicion or vagueness stalls it.
quests.culturalNote: At weddings, 'How do you know the couple?' is a standard opener to find common ground.

quests.instruction: Pick the response that fits the situation.
quests.scene: At a conference coffee break, two strangers are chatting and you'd like to join them.
options: You two look busy, sorry.
Mind if I join you? I'm Dev, I work in logistics.
Are you talking about the keynote?
I'll stand here in case you need a third.
quests.hint: Ask permission, then say who you are.
quests.explanation: Asking politely and introducing yourself makes joining feel welcome. Hovering or guessing at their topic feels awkward.
quests.culturalNote: Conferences invite mingling; a short opener with your name and field is standard.

quests.scene: At a party, a stranger asks 'What do you do?' You lost your job a month ago and are looking for design work.
options: Nothing, really.
I'm unemployed right now, so there's really not much to tell about my work life.
That's a bit personal for a party.
I'm between jobs at the moment — looking into design roles.
quests.hint: Be honest but frame it forward.
quests.explanation: Naming your search direction gives them something to respond to. Blunt or defensive answers close the topic.
quests.culturalNote: 'Between jobs' is a common, non-defensive way to describe unemployment; it isn't dishonest.

quests.scene: Your friend's partner, Priya, arrives at your dinner party. You haven't met her before.
options: Hi. Coats go on the bed.
You must be Priya — I've heard a lot about you. Let me take your coat.
Come in, dinner's not ready yet.
Are you the one who's vegetarian? I have to know before I plate everything up.
quests.hint: Welcome the person first, logistics second.
quests.explanation: Greeting her by name and offering to take her coat feels warm. Starting with logistics or diet questions feels impersonal.
quests.culturalNote: Hosts usually greet by name and offer coats as a way to make guests feel expected.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: You're meeting your partner's parents for the first time at their home.
options: Hey Mr. and Mrs. Kaur, cool house!
It's really nice to meet you both. Thank you for having me.
So, what was Jay like as a kid? I bet there are some really embarrassing stories.
Hello. Where should I sit?
quests.hint: You are a guest and first impressions matter.
quests.explanation: Politeness and thanks show respect for their hospitality. Being overfamiliar or transactional makes a poor first impression.
quests.culturalNote: Meeting parents often calls for slightly more formality than you would use with friends.

quests.scene: In a hostel kitchen, a traveler is cooking pasta as you walk in on your first evening.
options: Smells great! I'm Kai, just arrived today.
Are you using both burners?
You're in my spot.
Do you always cook this late at night, or is tonight a special occasion?
quests.hint: Start with something friendly, not something territorial.
quests.explanation: A compliment plus your name is inviting. Questions about the stove or territory feel confrontational.
quests.culturalNote: Hostel kitchens are social spaces; friendly openers are common.

quests.scene: Your class is doing introductions and you have thirty seconds to introduce yourself.
options: Hello. I'm Yuki. That's all, I guess.
My name is Yuki Tanaka, I have two brothers, a dog, and I was born in 2004.
Hi everyone, I'm Yuki. I'm studying biology and I love cycling.
I don't like introductions, but I'm Yuki.
quests.hint: Give a name and one or two interesting details.
quests.explanation: A name and a couple of facts give classmates hooks for conversation. Too little or too much or a complaint doesn't help.
quests.culturalNote: Self-introductions usually balance brevity with a personal touch.

quests.scene: You're calling a company you don't know about a job vacancy you saw online.
options: Hi, is this the place that's hiring?
Good afternoon, my name is Sam Lee. I'm calling about the assistant vacancy — is now a good time?
Yes, hello, I want a job.
Hello, can I speak to whoever is in charge of the hiring there? I saw an advert online this morning and I'd like to ask about it.
quests.hint: A professional call needs your name, your purpose, and a check on timing.
quests.explanation: Stating who you are, why you call, and checking timing respects the listener. The others are vague or blunt.
quests.culturalNote: Phone etiquette usually includes checking if it's a good time.

quests.scene: Your friend introduces you as 'Lin, an engineer' to a new contact, but you're actually a designer.
options: No, I'm not.
Actually, I'm a designer, though I work closely with engineers.
That's not true at all, you've got my job title completely wrong, I'm afraid.
Sure, something like that.
quests.hint: Correct it lightly so the new contact knows the truth.
quests.explanation: A light correction keeps things friendly and accurate. Blunt contradiction embarrasses your friend, and staying silent leaves a false impression.
quests.culturalNote: Small corrections during introductions are normal if made gently.

quests.scene: You're alone in the elevator with the CEO of your company, whom you've never spoken to.
options: Hey! Big boss!
Nice weather we're having, isn't it? Hopefully it stays like this all week.
Sorry, I'm not supposed to talk to you.
Good morning. I'm Hana from accounts — it's good to see you.
quests.hint: Be brief, respectful, and introduce yourself.
quests.explanation: A polite greeting with your name and department is professional and appropriate. Jokes or silence miss the chance.
quests.culturalNote: Many CEOs appreciate brief, respectful acknowledgement rather than either avoidance or overfamiliarity.

quests.scene: You arrive at a clinic's reception for a two o'clock appointment with Mr. Chen.
options: I'm here for Chen.
Is Mr. Chen ready to see me yet, or should I just sit down and wait somewhere?
Hello, I have a two o'clock appointment with Mr. Chen.
I'm early, so I'll just wait here.
quests.hint: State who you are here to see and when.
quests.explanation: Giving the time and full name lets reception find you quickly. Vague or presumptuous phrasing causes delay.
quests.culturalNote: Front-desk staff need the appointment time and the practitioner's name.

quests.scene: It's your first time visiting Professor Adeyemi's office hours. You're in her Tuesday class.
options: Hi, do you have a minute?
Hey prof, I'm Lucas from the Tuesday lecture, and I have a question about the last assignment.
Sorry to bother you, but...
Hello Professor Adeyemi, I'm Lucas from your Tuesday class — thanks for seeing me.
quests.hint: Professors see many students; help them place you.
quests.explanation: Naming yourself and your class helps her place you quickly. Vague or apologetic openers don't.
quests.culturalNote: Titles are generally used with professors until they suggest otherwise.

quests.scene: At a networking event, you've talked with someone for ten minutes and want to move on politely.
options: Well, I have to go now.
Okay, bye.
It was great talking with you. I'm going to say hello to a few others — enjoy the evening.
Someone else is waving at me over there, so sorry, I really have to run right now, bye.
quests.hint: Leave gracefully with a friendly closing.
quests.explanation: A warm closing with a reason keeps the connection positive. Abrupt exits or excuses feel rude.
quests.culturalNote: Networking events expect people to circulate; a polite exit is normal.

quests.scene: You've enjoyed a conversation with a potential mentor at a professional event and want to stay in touch.
options: It'd be great to keep in touch — could I get your email?
Give me your number.
Do you have LinkedIn or something?
We should totally hang out sometime, I'll find you on social media or something like that.
quests.hint: Ask directly and respectfully for a contact method.
quests.explanation: A polite, specific request fits a professional connection. Demands or vague invitations don't.
quests.culturalNote: Email is often the default contact in professional first meetings.

quests.scene: A senior client you've just met says, 'Please, call me Bill.'
options: I'd prefer to keep calling you Mr. Harris.
Thank you, Bill. Please call me Ana.
Okay, Mr. Bill.
Sure, whatever you like.
quests.hint: Accept warmly and offer yours in return.
quests.explanation: Accepting and offering your own name signals mutual comfort. Refusing or mixing forms awkwardly signals discomfort.
quests.culturalNote: When someone invites first names, accepting is a sign of trust in many English-speaking settings.

quests.scene: You run into an old friend at the supermarket after several years of no contact.
options: You've changed a lot.
It's been ages! I'm so glad we ran into each other. How have you been?
Wow. I barely recognized you.
Do you still work at the same place, or did you finally change jobs like you always wanted?
quests.hint: Lead with warmth, not observations about appearance.
quests.explanation: A warm reunion greeting opens the conversation positively. Comments on change can sound critical.
quests.culturalNote: Reunions usually open with warmth and an open question.

quests.scene: At your first badminton club session, the coach asks, 'Have you played before?' You've only played casually.
options: Yes, I'm pretty good, I played a lot at school so you don't need to explain the rules.
Not really, I don't think I can.
A little — mostly casually, so I'll need some pointers.
That depends what you mean by played.
quests.hint: Give an honest level so he can help.
quests.explanation: An honest answer helps the coach place you. Overclaiming or evasion makes coaching harder.
quests.culturalNote: Coaches want an honest level; overselling can lead to a mismatch.

quests.scene: At a formal gala, the host greets you at the door.
options: Good evening. Thank you for the invitation — it's a lovely venue.
Hi, thanks. Where's the bar, and is there somewhere to leave our coats and bags?
Sorry we're late, traffic.
Am I dressed okay for this?
quests.hint: A guest's first words should thank and compliment.
quests.explanation: Thanking the host and complimenting the venue is gracious. Practical or self-focused comments miss the moment.
quests.culturalNote: Formal events call for polished greetings.

quests.scene: You're meeting an online friend in person for the first time at a train station.
options: You look a bit different from your photos, but I guess everyone does in real life.
So are we going to eat or what?
This is weird, isn't it?
Hi! It's so good to finally meet you in person.
quests.hint: Express warmth about finally meeting.
quests.explanation: Expressing warmth sets a positive tone. Commenting on looks or awkwardness can make things uncomfortable.
quests.culturalNote: First in-person meetings after online friendships benefit from warmth.

quests.instruction: Choose the best way to respond.
quests.scene: You're a teacher at parent evening and Mr. Silva arrives for his appointment.
options: Good evening, Mr. Silva, thank you for coming. Please have a seat.
Hello, are you Marcus's dad?
Sit anywhere you like, I'll be with you shortly, I'm just finishing with another parent.
You're right on time — most parents are late.
quests.hint: Welcome parents by name and courteously.
quests.explanation: Greeting him by name and inviting him to sit feels respectful. Guessing identity or commenting on other parents doesn't.
quests.culturalNote: Parent-teacher meetings usually use formal titles.

quests.instruction: Pick the response that fits the situation.
quests.scene: At a party, a stranger says quietly, 'I don't know anyone here.'
options: Me neither — want to grab a drink and find a spot to talk?
That must be hard for you.
You should try meeting people.
I know pretty much everyone here, so just ask me if you want an introduction.
quests.hint: Match their honesty and offer company.
quests.explanation: Sharing the situation and inviting them creates connection. Pity or advice puts distance between you.
quests.culturalNote: Shared awkwardness is a good icebreaker.
